01 / ELECTRONIC STATES · S

What does a wavefunction describe?

At fixed nuclear positions, an electronic wavefunction assigns an amplitude to configurations of all electrons, including their spin labels. Its squared magnitude gives a probability density in many-electron configuration space—not a little electron orbit around a bond. An electronic state is an eigenstate of an approximate Hamiltonian; spin and antisymmetry constrain its allowed form.

H^eΨk=Ee,kΨk

Symbols: Ĥe is the electronic Hamiltonian (kinetic energy and Coulomb terms at fixed nuclei); Ψk is a normalized many-electron state; Ee,k is its electronic energy, commonly reported in hartree or eV. The nuclear repulsion term is added for the fixed-nuclei energy surface.

Organic example: ordinary SN2 is modeled as a closed-shell, paired-electron pathway. Radical addition requires an open-shell description; the S digit distinguishes these educational state classes, not a measured spin purity.

S · Electronic state in the codebook ↗
Assumptions and limits

In atomic units, Ĥe = −½Σi∇i² − Σi,AZA/riA + Σi<j1/rij: electron kinetic energy, electron–nuclear attraction and electron–electron repulsion. Indices i,j enumerate electrons, A nuclei; ZA is nuclear charge in proton-charge units, r distances in bohr, energy in hartree. The spin multiplicity 2S+1 uses total spin quantum number S. This is the nonrelativistic, fixed-nuclei picture. A molecular state is a many-electron object; a single orbital is not the entire wavefunction. Spin–orbit coupling, excited states, and multireference character may require richer treatments. An unrestricted broken-symmetry determinant is not necessarily an eigenfunction of total spin.

Conceptual occupancy · not a calculation
Paired model↑↓one spatial orbital · opposite spins
Open-shell model↑one unpaired electron · spin density may be distributed

Arrows here denote spin projections, not curved-arrow electron flow.

02 / ORBITALS & COUPLING · O

Overlap is not enough: energy matters.

An orbital representation expands each molecular orbital in basis functions. Matching spatial symmetry can permit interaction; energy separation and the off-diagonal coupling together set the mixing in an orthonormal two-state model. Move the controls to see avoided crossing and level repulsion. It is not an SN2 ab initio orbital calculation.

φj=∑μcμjχμ
H=(εDVV*εA),E±=εD+εA2±(Δ2)2+|V|2

Symbols: φj is an MO, χμ a basis function, cμj its coefficient. εD, εA, E±, Δ = εA − εD, and |V| have energy units (eV here); V = ⟨D|Ĥ|A⟩ may be complex. The display fixes εD = 0 and Δ ≥ 0. States |D⟩ and |A⟩ are orthonormal model states.

Organic example: backside donation toward σ*(C–Br) helps describe SN2; Diels–Alder involves a symmetry-allowed cyclic combination of π systems, not merely the same two-state interaction. O1 and O3 retain that distinction.

O · Orbital organization ↗
Assumptions and limits

The chosen diabatic states and coupling depend on representation and orthogonalization. A donor orbital/acceptor orbital matrix is a teaching analogy, not a uniquely defined electronic-state Hamiltonian for SN2. Kohn–Sham and Hartree–Fock orbital energies are model-dependent, not general ionization or excitation energies. Zero Δ and zero V leave an exact degeneracy with no unique mixing angle.

Analytic two-state model · eV

03 / DENSITY & BONDING · R

Phase is not charge.

An orbital amplitude can change sign across a node, but its probability density cannot be negative. Total electron density adds occupied-orbital contributions in a single-determinant picture; a difference density subtracts two specified states at mapped geometry and electron number. Positive Δρ means electron accumulation relative to the chosen reference, not a positively charged orbital lobe.

pj(r)=|φj(r)|2,ρ(r)≈∑jfjpj(r),Δρ=ρB−ρA

Symbols: r is position (Å or bohr for a molecular calculation); pj and ρ are probability/electron-number densities (Å⁻³ or bohr⁻³ in 3D), fj occupancy (electrons), A and B defined reference/target states. The toy plot uses one dimension, dimensionless x and density per unit x. A correlated many-electron density comes from integrating |Ψ|² over other electrons, not necessarily an orbital sum.

Organic example: a C–Br bond weakening and C–O bond formation in SN2 should be examined using matched geometries and an explicit density partition; a changed NBO or Mayer bond index depends on convention. R2 records replacement but not the density field or bond-order values.

R · Electronic reorganization ↗
Assumptions and limits

The phase of an orbital can be reversed globally without changing density. The plot uses normalized one-dimensional functions, not real molecular orbitals. Its two-electron bonding density and separated-reference density each integrate to two electrons, so the difference integrates to zero. Population charges, localization basins and bond orders require stated definitions and can disagree; no numerical SN2 density redistribution is asserted.

Normalized one-dimensional functions · illustrative

04 / REACTION LANDSCAPES · G

Nuclei move on an energy landscape.

In the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, solve the electronic problem for each fixed nuclear geometry R, then add nuclear repulsion to form a potential-energy surface (PES). A stationary point has zero gradient; a conventional minimum has positive curvature in vibrational directions and a first-order saddle has one negative-curvature direction. A path is a choice through that surface, not automatically an IRC.

U(R)=Ee(R)+VNN(R),∇RU=0

Symbols: R represents nuclear coordinates (normally Å or bohr); Ee, VNN, U are energies (hartree or eV); ∇RU is the gradient (energy/length); the Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives (energy/length² before mass weighting). The plotted x and y are dimensionless model coordinates.

Organic example: published Cl⁻ + CH₃Cl has a reactant complex and a symmetric TS on the gas-phase PES; our lesson surface is not fitted to those energies. G2 describes approach/departure geometry, not a barrier or trajectory.

G · Geometric pathway ↗
Assumptions and limits

The analytic model U(x,y) = A(x² − 1)² + By² has minima at (±1,0) and a saddle at (0,0), for A,B > 0. Its barrier from either minimum is A. This is a potential-energy surface, not Gibbs free energy or a dynamical simulation. Real TS validation requires an optimized geometry, one relevant imaginary vibrational mode (for a nondegenerate first-order saddle), and path connectivity checks such as an IRC; solvent and recrossing are additional questions.

Analytic 2D double well · not molecular data

05 / FROM PHYSICS TO A TEACHING INDEX

Four questions, not four observables.

SORG labels a proposed elementary-event model: S asks about electronic state; O about the dominant interaction organization; R about the bonding/electron reorganization; G about nuclear geometry. These are human-chosen summaries informed by evidence, not four eigenvalues derived from the Schrödinger equation.

(model,evidence)⟶interpretation(S,O,R,G)

Symbols: S, O, R and G are categorical labels without units; the arrow denotes judgment using a declared model and evidence, not a physical operator. Numerical categories remain the existing project codebook.

Worked comparison: SN2 (1122) has paired-electron displacement, backside donor–acceptor approach, and bond replacement. Thermal Diels–Alder (1333) has a concerted cyclic orbital organization and collective bond/geometry changes. Both are closed-shell in these teaching models, yet their pathways and orbital symmetry differ.

Compare existing event codes ↗
Where the map breaks

Different orbital partitions or coordinates can give different narratives. SORG omits energies, solvent, rates, stereoselectivity, spin contamination, asynchronous bond development and uncertainty. Candidate assignments remain candidates. No quantum-mechanical invariant or numerical similarity metric has been validated for the digits.

01 / THE CLASSIFICATION

Four questions, one code.

The code order is always S → O → R → G.
A shared code indicates coarse-grained similarities, not identical reactions.

∴
What guides this classification?

We describe each key mechanistic event using electronic state, donor–acceptor and frontier orbitals, electron-pair or single-electron movement, and nuclear geometry. SORG is a project-defined educational index, not a validated quantum-mechanical invariant or an IUPAC standard. The O and R boundaries remain open to revision. An orbital decomposition must state its orbital basis and fragment convention.

Read the assignment rules ↗
READ AN EXAMPLEWhy do SN2 and proton transfer both map to 1122?

Both are closed-shell donor–acceptor events. One bond is replaced by another as approach and departure are coupled. The reaction center and orbital details belong to the mechanism description.

06 / METHOD & EVIDENCE

Ground each simplification
and make its limits visible.

Describe reactions through electronic state, orbital coupling, electron reorganization, and nuclear motion.
Mechanisms and verified electronic-structure results are central; missing results remain labeled as such.

01

One event, one code

Assign codes to elementary-event models. Explicitly labeled grouped stages are provisional summaries, not single elementary events. Preserve repeated codes: SN1 ionization and capture are both 1111; water as the nucleophile also requires a 1122 deprotonation. Resonance forms and multiple arrows within one event do not add steps.

02

Codes are hypotheses to test

SORG organizes reactions by electronic state, orbital interactions, bond reorganization, and geometry. It is an educational approximation, not a validated quantum-mechanical invariant or IUPAC standard. A shared code cannot replace molecular-orbital or electronic-structure data. A two-component mathematical example can change participation ratio from 2 to 1 under a basis rotation; this is an illustration of representation dependence, not a reaction calculation. S, O, R, and G are related descriptions, not independent physical observables.

03

Quantum data require a method

Specify molecular identity, conformation, charge and spin, solvent, electronic-structure method, basis and fragment convention. The SN2 and Diels–Alder cards show sourced numerical cases; further cards give sourced qualitative conclusions. Every card separately states a proposed calculation for its teaching substrate. Published calculations for analogous models are identified as such.

Inspect methods and published conclusions

Open Data & calculations on any reaction for its proposed protocol. See numerical models on SN2 ↗ and Diels–Alder ↗; see primary-study conclusions on E2 ↗, SN1/SN2 boundary ↗, carbonyl attack ↗, Claisen ↗, and nitration ↗.

Computational workflow and what each method can establish ＋

1. Define a molecular model

Write the exact substrate, nucleophile, charge, spin, counterion, solvent and conformers. Explicit solvent clusters and continuum models answer different questions; compare plausible arrangements.

2. Verify the path

Optimize reactant, intermediate, transition and product structures using a stated DFT or wavefunction method and basis. A minimum has no imaginary frequency; a conventional first-order saddle has one. Follow the intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) in both directions to test local connectivity. Recheck key electronic energies at a suitable higher level when feasible.

3. Analyze electrons

Report bond lengths, density, spin density and bond orders along the same path. Activation strain separates deformation from interaction at a chosen geometry. EDA subdivides the interaction for declared fragments. ELF tracks changes in electron localization. Orbital energies, NBO donor–acceptor terms and population charges depend on their chosen representation.

4. Define coupling carefully

For an electron-transfer question, construct donor/acceptor diabatic states at identical nuclear geometry and state a method such as generalized Mulliken–Hush, with orthogonalization and solvent conventions. HDA has energy units; orbital overlap is dimensionless. Report basis, conformer, solvation and electronic-state sensitivity instead of treating an EDA orbital term as the same coupling.

These steps are a research protocol, not computations performed by this atlas. An IRC does not prove that solvent dynamics follow a single trajectory. Any numerical result on a reaction card states its actual model and method.

Current scope

The atlas focuses on foundational polar reactions, radical-chain events, and thermal pericyclic reactions. Excited-state S3 and O4/R4 electron-transfer cases remain in the codebook but are not yet assigned. Published radical-cation Diels–Alder data are discussed as a comparison, not assigned the neutral reaction’s code. Metal aggregation, explicit solvent participation, and full reaction networks are not yet covered; each entry states its scope.

07 / RESEARCH & METHODS

An SN2 model with
traceable numbers.

Cl⁻ + CH₃Cl in the gas phase is a published identity-substitution model—not the HO⁻ + CH₃Br equation in the teaching card. Select a reported state, inspect what was calculated, and see what remains unavailable.

Published ZORA-OLYP/TZ2P/ADF · no Atlas quantum calculationThree tabulated states, not interpolated IRC frames. The authors report IRC and frequency validation; this viewer does not replay sampled coordinates.
Why orbital interaction matters ↗Phase, density and missing bond orders ↗What the energy points mean ↗What 1122 leaves out ↗

Backside attack and 1122

Chloride 3p donation into the backside lobe of σ*(C–Clout) accompanies bond formation and departure. At the symmetric transition state, both C–Cl distances are 2.351 Å. SORG 1122 indexes the closed-shell displacement and approach–departure exchange, but not orbital energy, strain, the reactant-complex well or atom identity.

Energy and method boundary

Relative electronic energies are 0 (separated reactants), −9.2 (reactant complex) and −0.3 kcal mol⁻¹ (transition state). The TS has +31.6 strain and −31.9 kcal mol⁻¹ interaction under the paper's Cl⁻/CH₃Cl fragment convention. The RC-to-TS difference is 8.9 kcal mol⁻¹ by subtraction, not a separately tabulated value or solution free-energy barrier.

Density and bond-order gap

The isolated substrate σ* energy is −5.13 eV and its VDD carbon charge is −0.031 e; the TS fragment-orbital overlap is 0.215 (dimensionless). These do not form a charge-transfer or bond-order trajectory. Numerical bond-order evolution, RC/TS density changes, full checked Cartesian frames and continuous IRC energies are unavailable here.
